rv.q: Its clarified, minimalist, definitive beauty leaps down your throat and into your heart.

The best good news about “Here We Are,” the combo platter Buñuel musical that opened on Sunday at the Shed, nearly two years after Sondheim’s death in November 2021, is that it justifies the idea of merging these two works and succeeds in making a surrealist musical expressive.
Setting aside that hallowed status as the Last Sondheim Musical, assessing the show on its merits, it is an almost continuously deranged delight.
Here We Are is meticulously assembled—including by choreographer Sam Pinkleton, lighting designer Natasha Katz, and sound designer Tom Gibbons—as well as cleverly written and wonderfully performed.

When it wobbles, and it does so increasingly as it goes along, it’s not because it began without a clear proposition: It’s because the logical conclusion of its premise is in fact so dark, so extreme, that you can feel the opposing, more compassionate (or at least more ambivalent)
Despite the multivalent talents of Ives and Mantello, though, the piece, finished without Sondheim, cannot mend the ragged edge torn by his absence.
The resulting evening might not be stranded at square one, but it doesn’t satisfactorily cross the finish line, either.
But the combination of Sondheim’s score with Ives’ absurd and often hilarious book, rather than generating synergy, feels uneasy and disjointed, like they’re pulling in opposite directions.
The novelty of attending Sondheim’s final musical and experiencing its non-stop zaniness wear off long before “Here We Are” ends, and the whole thing falls apart.
It adds a zap of electricity to the theatre season, thanks to inspired work by a dream cast and ace designers who serve up a slim slice of surrealism under Joe Mantello's (Wicked) direction.
With his final offering, Sondheim sends one last jolt of structural inventiveness coursing through the veins of the musical theater form.
It’s a surrealist puzzle that Sondheim and Ives clearly enjoyed trying to solve — and we’d be hard-pressed not to enjoy it ourselves.
“Here We Are” is worth the investment.
But if Here We Are remains an unfinished work, it still has plenty to offer, especially in Mantello's lovingly realized production...
What music there is, is playful and joyous.

With David Ives’ clever book, Joe Mantello’s ever-flowing direction, a cast of amazing reliables,and David Zinn’s versatile and attractive set design in the Shed’s Griffin Theater, Here We Are is exciting and challenging theater.
"Here We Are" is a stylish, committed production of an incomplete, flawed work. That is no terrible thing—scraps of wonderful Sondheim are still worth more than much other theater.
Long-gestating, long-awaited, “Here We Are” can itself be considered wonderful just for existing, like an unexpected visit from an old friend.

That we’re seeing the musical at all is truly fortunate since even minor Sondheim, which in my estimation this piece feels like on a single viewing (always risky when it comes to his work), puts most other composers to shame.
If not necessarily compelling, it is merrily quirky and often interesting, with jagged chords and intricately rhythmic exchanges.
Not precisely a non finito musical but nevertheless a semi-masterpiece, Here We Are benefits from sensationally chic design...
While the attempt is not without merit, its achievements can only be considered such with a healthy dose of prefab admiration.
Meanwhile, for lovers of Sondheim and musical theater, it is imperative to see this vibrant production of Here We Are at The Shed, filled with vitality and creativity.
This was a show that fully grasped these concepts.
Theater Stephen Sondheim's 'Here We Are' ends on a surreal note (Off Broadway review) Date: October 23, 2023.
Now grab a chair and bite into this enormously fun and flavourful romp.
Although "Here We Are" leaves you hungry for completion, it's a slow-crawling nightmare that plink-pla-plink in your consciousness long after you leave the theatre.

cn.t: Sondheim's unfinished final musical divides critics between those celebrating the master's brilliant Act One and inventive concept, and those disappointed by its incomplete second act and surrealist excesses.
